concepts.title: Sources of Data: Primary and Secondary

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Sources of Data: Primary and Secondary' refers to.
questions.a: Primary data is collected first-hand by the investigator for a specific purpose, while secondary data is obtained from already published or existing sources such as reports, journals, and government publications.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Sources of Data: Primary and Secondary'.
questions.a: Primary data is original and collected for the current study; secondary data is borrowed from existing sources.

questions.q: Give one standard exam phrasing that targets 'Sources of Data: Primary and Secondary'.
questions.a: What are the sources of data in statistics?

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Methods of Collecting Primary Data' refers to.
questions.a: Primary data can be collected through direct personal investigation, indirect oral investigation, information from local sources or correspondents, mailed questionnaires, and telephonic interviews.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Methods of Collecting Primary Data'.
questions.a: The choice of method depends on the purpose, budget, time, and the nature of the respondents.

questions.q: Give one standard exam phrasing that targets 'Methods of Collecting Primary Data'.
questions.a: What are the main methods of collecting primary data?

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Census and Sampling Methods' refers to.
questions.a: The census method collects data from every unit of the population, while the sampling method collects data from a selected representative part (sample) of the population and generalises the results.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Census and Sampling Methods'.
questions.a: Census gives complete and accurate data but is costly; sampling is economical and faster but results are estimates.

questions.q: Give one standard exam phrasing that targets 'Census and Sampling Methods'.
questions.a: What is the difference between census and sampling?

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Frequency Distribution' refers to.
questions.a: A frequency distribution is a tabular arrangement of data showing the number of observations (frequency) falling within each class or category.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Frequency Distribution'.
questions.a: A frequency distribution groups raw data into classes and counts how many observations fall in each class.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Frequency Distribution', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: frequency of class = count of observations in that class

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Types of Variables' refers to.
questions.a: A variable is a characteristic that can take different values. Discrete variables take only whole number values (like number of children), while continuous variables can take any value within a range (like height or weight).

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Types of Variables'.
questions.a: Discrete variables have gaps between values; continuous variables can take any fractional value within an interval.

questions.q: Give one standard exam phrasing that targets 'Types of Variables'.
questions.a: What is a variable in statistics?

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Tabular Presentation of Data' refers to.
questions.a: Tabular presentation is the systematic arrangement of data in rows and columns, usually with a title, stub (row headings), caption (column headings), body, and source note.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Tabular Presentation of Data'.
questions.a: A table organises data into rows and columns so that comparisons and relationships can be seen at a glance.

questions.q: Give one standard exam phrasing that targets 'Tabular Presentation of Data'.
questions.a: What is tabular presentation of data?

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Bar Diagrams' refers to.
questions.a: A bar diagram is a visual presentation of data using rectangular bars of equal width whose heights or lengths are proportional to the values they represent.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Bar Diagrams'.
questions.a: Bar diagrams compare values across categories using bars of equal width with heights proportional to the values.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Bar Diagrams', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: height of bar = value represented (to a chosen scale)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Pie Diagram' refers to.
questions.a: A pie diagram is a circular diagram in which the circle is divided into sectors, and the angle of each sector is proportional to the value it represents out of the total.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Pie Diagram'.
questions.a: A pie diagram shows the share of each component as a sector of a circle, where the full circle (360 degrees) represents the total.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Pie Diagram', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: angle of sector = (value / total) * 360

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Histogram and Frequency Polygon' refers to.
questions.a: A histogram is a bar diagram of a frequency distribution in which bars are drawn for each class interval with no gaps between them, and their heights represent the class frequencies. A frequency polygon is formed by joining the midpoints of the tops of the bars of a histogram with straight lines.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Histogram and Frequency Polygon'.
questions.a: A histogram shows the shape of a frequency distribution using adjacent bars; a frequency polygon connects the midpoints of those bars.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Histogram and Frequency Polygon', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: area of bar = class_width * frequency (for equal class widths, height = frequency)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Ogive and Time Series Graphs' refers to.
questions.a: An ogive is a cumulative frequency curve drawn by plotting cumulative frequencies against the upper or lower class boundaries. A time series graph plots values of a variable against time to show how it changes over a period.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Ogive and Time Series Graphs'.
questions.a: An ogive shows cumulative totals and helps find the median; a time series graph shows the trend of a variable over time.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Ogive and Time Series Graphs', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: cumulative frequency = running total of frequencies up to that class
